strengths: Addresses practical problem: Mesh-based generative editing is understudied despite being critical for professional 3D workflows
Intuitive and well-motivated pipeline: Decomposing into 2D editing → 3D generation → seamless fusion effectively leverages complementary model strengths
Sound technical design: Hybrid SDF/Mesh representation jointly optimizing geometry and appearance is well-thought-out, with principled Poisson blending and texture harmonization strategies
Consistent quantitative improvements: Shows gains across all metrics (CLIPsim +2.4, CLIPdir +5.4, NIQE -0.6, NIMA +0.2) compared to competitive baselines
Comprehensive component validation: Thorough ablation studies (Section 4.5) demonstrate importance of both geometry and texture components with per-loss analysis
Versatility demonstrated: Extension to drag-based editing shows framework generalization beyond text-based control
Clear presentation: Well-written with informative figures effectively communicating the pipeline and results
weaknesses: Critically limited evaluation dataset: Only 6 objects is far below CVPR standards; insufficient to assess generalization, failure modes, or robustness across diverse geometries and editing scenarios

Missing key implementation details: Edited region mesh extraction (Section 3.1) is vaguely described; alignment between Me and Mt unclear; hyperparameter selection (ε₀, ε₁, δ, λ weights) not justified; no sensitivity analysis provided

Incremental technical novelty: Primarily integrates classical techniques (Poisson Image Editing from 2003, hybrid SDF/Mesh from MagicClay [2], standard neural color fields); no fundamental algorithmic innovation introduced

Inappropriate evaluation metrics: CLIPsim/CLIPdir and NIQE/NIMA are proxy/image-quality metrics, not geometry-aware measures; cannot validate mesh fidelity claims without geometric consistency metrics or user studies

Heavy dependency on proprietary external models: Quality bottlenecked by FLUX Kontext and MeshyAI; reproducibility severely compromised as MeshyAI is a commercial API; no evidence method exceeds underlying models
Insufficient ablation coverage: No ablation on reference mesh guidance strategy, SDF vs. direct optimization, or hyperparameter sensitivity; only partial texture loss component analysis

Inadequate failure characterization: Minimal limitation discussion; no systematic analysis of failure modes (thin structures, multi-component meshes, noisy surfaces); cherry-picked success examples in Fig. 4 with baseline 'Fail' labels but no CraftMesh failures shown
Unsupported PBR materials claim: Paper claims direct extension to PBR rendering but provides zero experimental evidence—all results appear albedo-only
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, significance tests, or confidence intervals despite small n=6 sample size; quantitative improvements lack statistical validation
Incomplete comparisons: Recent 3D-native models (Clay, Hunyuan3D, Trellis) discussed in related work but not compared; MaskedLRM mentioned but omitted from evaluation
Limited drag-based evaluation: Only 2 simple examples with minimal analysis; claims of 'strong generalization potential' unsupported
Reproducibility concerns: Code promised post-acceptance; critical hyperparameters and dataset construction unexplained; dependency on proprietary APIs limits independent validation

strengths: Well-executed practical system combining 2D image editing and 3D mesh generation through principled Poisson-based fusion; addresses an important problem in professional 3D content creation where mesh editing has received limited attention

Elegant computational approach using 2D Poisson blending on normal maps (O(kn²)) instead of 3D volumetric solving (O(n³)), with novel distribution-aware color alignment solving real gradient-domain texture pattern interference

Comprehensive experimental validation with consistent improvements across multiple metrics (CLIPsim +3.0, CLIPdir +7.997 vs baselines), thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution, and robustness across three different mesh generation backends
Clear presentation of three-stage pipeline with good qualitative results (Figure 4) showing superiority on challenging editing tasks like deletion-fill and complex geometric modifications
Versatile framework supporting both text-based and drag-based editing modalities with demonstrated adaptability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily an engineering contribution adapting classical Poisson Image Editing (2003) to normal maps, with hybrid SDF/Mesh representation borrowed from MagicClay [2]; core innovation is modest

Insufficient evaluation rigor: only 100 models with 300 test cases (relatively small); no human studies despite claims of 'high-fidelity' and 'structural harmony'; metrics (CLIPsim, CLIPdir) measure semantic alignment with text, not geometric fidelity or structural preservation directly; missing simple baselines (Boolean-only, basic blending)

Incomplete technical justification: claim that 'implicit SDF effectively resolves inconsistencies' in multi-view-inconsistent normal maps lacks theoretical or empirical support; parameter sensitivity analysis absent (ε₀, ε₁, δ, σ, γ, λ₁, λ₂, θ₁, θ₂); unclear why SDF optimization works better than direct normal consistency

Reproducibility concerns: heavy dependence on proprietary/commercial models (FLUX Kontext, MeshyAI) with limited availability; no code release mentioned; many hyperparameters introduced without systematic justification or tuning protocol; implementation details sparse
Computational efficiency not addressed: ~6 minutes per edit on RTX 4090 (excluding mesh generation); no cost comparison with baselines; practical workflow overhead not discussed

Inconsistent results unclear: Table 2 shows large performance jump (+6.5 CLIPdir) from baseline to full method—is this from MeshyAI quality alone or the fusion? Different backends yield different performance, suggesting generative model quality dominates the contribution

Weak failure analysis: only 2 failure cases shown; systematic failure characterization missing; limitations section mentions problematic cases (open/layered/noisy surfaces) but provides no evidence; no statistics on success rates by editing type or object category
